text: Chapter 4's entire cost function leaned on one unexamined number: "predicted ETA between a driver and a rider." This chapter opens that box. A GPS point is not a location on a road — it's a noisy estimate near one. And a road network is not a plane you can measure with a ruler — it's a graph with one-way streets, bridges, and a finite number of ways across a river. Getting from "two dots on a map" to "a trustworthy number of seconds" requires two real algorithmic problems, solved at a speed dispatch can actually afford.

You will be able to Explain why straight-line distance and even raw GPS points are structurally the wrong inputs for ETA. You will understand Why naive Dijkstra over a full city road graph is too slow for real-time dispatch, and what contraction hierarchies do about it. You will predict The real speedup a precomputed hierarchy buys over a plain shortest-path search, with real complexity math. You will simulate Dijkstra's search frontier expanding node by node, then compare its work against a precomputed-shortcut query on the identical graph.

Every chapter so far has quietly used the phrase "predicted ETA" as if it were a single lookup. It is actually two distinct, hard problems stacked on top of each other, and conflating them is where naive implementations go wrong first.

Problem 1 — map matching. A phone's GPS reports a noisy point: accurate to maybe 5–20 meters under good conditions, far worse near tall buildings ("urban canyon" multipath reflection) or under tree cover. Before you can ask "what's the fastest route from here," you must answer a prior question: which road segment is this vehicle actually on? A raw GPS point 8 meters from a highway is ambiguous — it could be on the highway, or on a frontage road running parallel to it, and those two answers imply very different valid routes and speeds. Problem 2 — shortest path over a graph, with real-world weights. Once you know which road segment a vehicle is on, "closest" or "fastest" has to be computed over the actual road network — a graph of intersections and street segments, with one-way restrictions, turn penalties, and speed limits — not over open space. And the weight on each edge should reflect current conditions, not a fixed distance: a road that takes 40 seconds to cross at 2am can take 4 minutes during rush hour.

Recall chapter 4's cost function: cost(rider, driver) = ETA_seconds(...). Every claim chapter 4 made about batched assignment beating greedy depended on that ETA being a trustworthy measure of real travel time — if it were secretly straight-line distance, the "optimal" assignment computed by an exact solver would just be optimally wrong. This chapter is what makes chapter 4's central assumption actually true in a real system, and it has to do so fast enough that computing it for every candidate edge in a dispatch batch doesn't itself become the bottleneck.

Unlike H3 or the dispatch-matching problem, the core algorithms this chapter relies on predate Uber by decades — ride-hailing is a demanding consumer of shortest-path research, not its origin. Click through the milestones that made real-time, road-aware ETA computation possible at consumer-app latency.

Dijkstra's algorithm, A*, and contraction hierarchies are all published, peer-reviewed, publicly available techniques — you can read the original papers. What is not public is the exact routing engine Uber runs in production today: whether it's built in-house, which speedup technique(s) it uses, and how live traffic is blended in are not disclosed in the way H3's source code was. This chapter teaches the real, well-established public techniques any company at this scale needs, and is explicit about that boundary rather than presenting a guess as documented fact. Where a concrete example of an open-source system is useful, this chapter references OSRM (Open Source Routing Machine), a real, publicly available project that implements contraction hierarchies, as an illustration of the general technique — not as a claim about what Uber runs.
Two naive attempts, worth separating because they fail differently.

This is the metric chapter 4 warned about. It's cheap — O(1), no graph, no lookup — and it's wrong in exactly the systematic way that matters: it can't see rivers, highways, one-way streets, or traffic, so it's wrong hardest precisely where getting it right would matter most.

The "obviously correct" fix: model the city as a graph (intersections as nodes, street segments as weighted edges) and run Dijkstra's algorithm from the driver's node, expanding outward until the rider's node is reached. This is genuinely correct — it will find the true shortest path by construction — and it is the right first instinct once you know straight-line distance is wrong. Watch what happens when you have to run it thousands of times per second.

Short queries are cheap even naively. When origin and destination are close, Dijkstra's expanding frontier reaches the target after touching only a small neighborhood. This is the case that makes naive per-query search look fine in a demo.

Long queries are not a linear step up — they're much worse. Dijkstra's frontier grows roughly with the area it has to cover, and area grows with the square of distance on a roughly planar road network. A 28× longer query touches thousands of times more nodes, not 28× more.

Multiply by chapter 4's actual workload. A single dispatch batch needs an ETA for every candidate edge, and chapter 4's batch window is measured in hundreds of milliseconds, not seconds. Naive per-query Dijkstra alone can exceed the entire window's time budget before the assignment solver even starts.

Nothing is algorithmically wrong with plain Dijkstra. It's simply solving the whole problem fresh, from scratch, on every single query — exactly the "no precomputation, no cache" pattern that fails at any real query volume. §5 keeps its correctness guarantee while attacking the "solve from scratch every time" assumption directly.

Dijkstra's algorithm from a source node, run to completion (or until the target is popped from the priority queue), visits nodes in increasing order of distance from the source — its worst-case complexity is O((V + E) log V) with a binary-heap priority queue, where V is the number of intersections and E the number of street segments in the graph being searched. On a real city road graph, that's not an abstract cost:

City-scale graphs are large. A single dense metro area's drivable road network commonly has on the order of hundreds of thousands to low millions of nodes and a similar or larger number of edges. Even at O((V+E) log V), that's real, non-trivial work per query — milliseconds to tens of milliseconds depending on how far apart the two points are, not microseconds. You don't need one query — you need thousands per second. Chapter 4's candidate generation needs an ETA for every plausible rider×driver pair in every dispatch batch, across every active city, continuously. Multiply a per-query cost that's already measured in milliseconds by that volume, and plain per-query Dijkstra becomes the dominant cost of the entire dispatch pipeline — exactly the bottleneck chapter 4's §6 warned candidate generation could become if routing queries weren't cheap. Far-apart queries are the worst case, and they're common. Dijkstra's search frontier grows roughly with the area covered — a query between two points 15 km apart explores dramatically more of the graph than one between two points 500 m apart, so the naive approach's cost is least predictable exactly when demand is spread out (a driver on the edge of a service area, an airport pickup) rather than when it's dense.

Treat a mid-size city graph as ~500,000 nodes and ~1.2 million edges. Even a well-implemented Dijkstra with a binary heap does work proportional to (V+E)·log(V) ≈ 1.7M × ~19 ≈ 32 million priority-queue operations in the worst case to fully settle the graph — in practice a targeted query to one destination terminates earlier, but a query between two far-apart points on a large, densely connected graph can still legitimately touch hundreds of thousands of nodes before it's done. At even a modest fraction of a millisecond per node visited, a single long-distance query measured in tens of milliseconds, repeated for every candidate pair in every dispatch batch (chapter 4), quickly dominates the whole pipeline's latency budget. Something has to be precomputed ahead of time so that queries, not the whole graph, stay cheap.
Two independent fixes, one for each of §1's two problems.

Naively snapping a GPS point to its geometrically nearest road segment fails in exactly the cases that matter: a point near a highway and a parallel frontage road is genuinely ambiguous from one point alone. The well-established public technique — described in Newson & Krumm's 2009 paper "Hidden Markov Map Matching Through Noise and Sparseness" — treats map-matching as inference over a sequence of GPS points, not a single-point lookup: each candidate road segment is a hidden state, GPS accuracy gives an emission probability (how likely is this reading given the vehicle is really on this segment), and the road graph's connectivity gives transition probabilities (how likely is a real vehicle to have moved from segment A to segment B between two readings). The most likely sequence of road segments across several GPS points, not just the closest single segment to one point, is what map-matching actually solves for.

A* search (Hart, Nilsson & Raphael, 1968) is the first real speedup: it's Dijkstra with a heuristic that estimates remaining distance to the goal, so the search expands nodes in a direction biased toward the destination rather than uniformly outward in every direction. It helps — often substantially — but its worst-case complexity is still driven by graph size, because the heuristic only prioritizes exploration order, it doesn't reduce the graph itself.

Contraction hierarchies (Geisberger, Sanders, Schultes & Delling, 2008) take a fundamentally different approach: precompute, offline, a hierarchy of "shortcut" edges that represent the shortest path through unimportant intermediate nodes, ranked by importance (a highway interchange is far more important than a residential cul-de-sac). At query time, a bidirectional search that only needs to explore upward into more important shortcuts converges dramatically faster than a full Dijkstra over the original graph — because most of the "boring" middle of a long route was already collapsed into a handful of precomputed shortcuts long before any query happened.

Step 1 — importance ranking, computed once, offline. A heuristic estimates how "central" each node is to shortest paths generally — highway interchanges rank far above residential dead-ends. This ranking is the whole hierarchy's foundation and is expensive to compute well, which is exactly why it's done ahead of time, not per query.

Step 2 — contract nodes from least to most important. Removing a node and replacing its role with a direct shortcut edge (when needed to preserve shortest-path distances between its neighbors) is what actually shrinks the graph the online query has to deal with — most of a city's nodes are low-importance and get folded away this same way.

What you're left with is the original graph plus a relatively small number of extra "shortcut" edges that each silently represent a whole shortest path through now-removed nodes. Nothing about the original road network was deleted — the hierarchy is an addition, not a replacement.

The payoff. A query only has to climb "upward" through increasingly important shortcuts from both ends until the two searches meet — it never has to fan out across the low-importance nodes that were folded away, because their shortest-path contribution is already baked into the shortcuts it's climbing through. §8's slider computes exactly how few nodes this touches versus plain Dijkstra.

OSRM (Open Source Routing Machine) is a real, publicly available open-source routing engine that implements contraction hierarchies over OpenStreetMap data, and its published benchmarks are a genuine, citable example of the speedup class this technique buys: queries answered in single-digit milliseconds on continent-scale road graphs, after an offline preprocessing pass that can take minutes to hours depending on graph size. This chapter uses OSRM as an honest, real illustration of the general technique — it is not a claim about what routing engine Uber itself runs internally, which isn't public.

Preprocessing cost and staleness. A contraction hierarchy is built offline against a snapshot of the road graph — new roads, closures, and construction all mean the precomputed hierarchy is stale until it's rebuilt, and rebuilding a continent-scale hierarchy is not instantaneous. A routing engine has to decide how to handle the gap between "the world changed" and "the hierarchy caught up." Static shortcuts assume static weights — but traffic isn't static. The entire point of contraction hierarchies is precomputing shortest paths through unimportant nodes ahead of time — but "shortest" depends on edge weights, and if those weights are travel times that change by the hour (rush hour vs. 2am) or the minute (an accident just happened), a hierarchy built against one weight snapshot can recommend a route that is no longer actually fastest. Incorporating live, time-varying traffic into a structure engineered around precomputed static shortcuts is a genuinely hard, actively-studied systems problem — one honest answer is recomputing or partially updating hierarchies on faster cycles for the weights that change fastest, and leaning on structural shortcuts (which change rarely) plus a live traffic-weighted final pass near the query time. Map-matching still costs real computation per GPS ping. Chapter 3 established that a real driver fleet generates a continuous, large-volume ping stream; every one of those pings needs a map-matching pass to keep dispatch's model of "which road segment is this driver actually on" current, which is nontrivial recurring work layered on top of chapter 3's ingestion pipeline, not a one-time cost. None of this eliminates the underlying graph-search complexity class — it amortizes it. Contraction hierarchies don't make shortest-path search polynomially cheaper in a complexity-theory sense; they trade a large one-time (and periodically repeated) offline cost for a much smaller online cost per query. That's the right trade for a system answering millions of queries against a graph that changes slowly relative to query volume — but it is a trade, not a free win.

A real-time, traffic-aware, always-current shortest path over a road network the size of a metro area is a genuinely hard, still-actively-researched systems problem. Every production routing engine at this scale is making deliberate engineering tradeoffs between hierarchy freshness, traffic-data freshness, and query latency — there is no configuration that makes all three perfect simultaneously, and this chapter does not pretend otherwise.

A routing query needs a graph node to start from — not a raw lat/lon. Running map-matching as a distinct upstream stage, rather than folding "guess the nearest road" logic into the router itself, means the router can assume clean graph-node inputs and stay focused purely on the shortest-path problem, while map-matching can independently improve its own accuracy (better GPS noise models, more context from recent pings) without touching routing logic at all — the same separation-of-concerns instinct chapter 4 applied to its own pipeline stages.

Three pieces: (a) A* as a concrete, implementable improvement over plain Dijkstra, (b) the contraction-hierarchy query in more mechanical detail, (c) a slider that computes the real relative search cost for both approaches on a generated grid graph, not an assumed curve.

The heuristic must be admissible for A* to guarantee the true shortest path, not merely a good-looking one — straight-line distance divided by the fastest possible speed on any road is a standard, safe choice, because no real route can ever be faster than that theoretical bound.

Offline, every node is assigned an importance rank and "contracted" in rank order — removed from the graph after adding shortcut edges that preserve shortest-path distances between its remaining neighbors. Online, a query runs a bidirectional search — forward from the origin, backward from the destination — where each direction is only allowed to relax edges going up in rank. The two searches meet at some high-rank node, and because most of any long route's "boring middle" was already collapsed into a few shortcuts spanning important highway-like nodes, the search touches vastly fewer nodes than a full Dijkstra over the original graph.

Two searches start simultaneously, one from each endpoint, each restricted to relaxing only edges that go up in contraction rank — a small fraction of the total edges touching any given node, because most of its neighbors were already contracted away below it.

Both directions climb fast. Within a handful of hops, each search reaches nodes with almost no further "upward" edges to explore except the big precomputed shortcuts — this is where the earlier contraction pass is doing its work silently, in the background, for free at query time.

The two searches meet at some shared high-importance node — commonly something like a major highway interchange for a long cross-town query. Neither search had to reach all the way to the other endpoint; they only needed to reach each other.

Unpack for the final answer. The query itself only worked with compact shortcut edges — turning that into an actual turn-by-turn route means recursively expanding each shortcut back into the real road segments it stands for. The travel-time NUMBER was correct the whole time; this step is only needed if you also want driving directions, not just an ETA.

The pattern repeats from chapters 1 and 4: every strategy trades query latency against freshness and implementation complexity — none escapes the tradeoff, they just place it differently. Contraction hierarchies are the standard textbook answer for "fast queries over a slowly-changing graph"; techniques like CRP exist specifically because production routing needs the graph's topology to stay stable while its weights (live traffic) change constantly, which plain contraction hierarchies handle awkwardly.

Plain Dijkstra / A*: O((V+E) log V) worst case; in practice, a single query's real cost scales with how many nodes lie within the search frontier before the target is reached — roughly proportional to the area the search has to cover, which grows with the square of query distance on a roughly planar road network. Contraction hierarchies: offline preprocessing is superlinear in graph size (computing an optimal contraction order is itself a hard optimization problem approximated heuristically) but is a one-time or periodic cost; online queries commonly touch a number of nodes on the order of hundreds, largely independent of total graph size, because the search only needs to climb into a small set of high-importance shortcuts regardless of how large the underlying graph is. Map-matching: per-ping cost is small and roughly constant (a local search over a handful of nearby candidate road segments plus a probability update), but it runs continuously against chapter 3's full ping volume — it's a steady-state tax, not a rare one-off. What this buys chapter 4 concretely: a routing engine answering ETA queries in single-digit milliseconds, rather than tens of milliseconds, is the difference between candidate generation being a minor contributor to batch latency versus being the dominant one.

The curves are an analytic sketch — plain search cost growing with graph size, hierarchy query cost staying close to flat — chosen to be qualitatively consistent with published contraction-hierarchy results (query costs that are near-independent of total graph size is the technique's whole point) rather than a claim about any specific production system's measured numbers.

Ride-hailing apps across the industry have, at various points, been the subject of user complaints and press coverage about displayed ETAs that consistently ran optimistic compared to actual arrival — riders reporting "3 minutes" turning into 8 or 10. No specific internal Uber postmortem for this is public, so this chapter does not attribute a specific cause with false precision, but the general, well-documented mechanism this class of bug follows is exactly this chapter's subject: an ETA pipeline relying on stale or under-weighted traffic data, or a routing hierarchy answering queries against pre-rush-hour weights, will produce numbers that were true when the weights were computed and false by the time the vehicle actually drives the route. The general fix — the honest answer any engineer at this scale gives — is treating live-traffic freshness as a first-class SLO on the routing pipeline, not just an accuracy nice-to-have.

Consumer GPS-navigation history broadly (not specific to any one ride-hailing company) is full of well-known, publicly documented incidents where routing engines directed vehicles onto unsuitable roads — closed roads, private property, unpaved tracks — because the underlying map data was wrong or stale, and the shortest-path search faithfully found the "shortest" route through bad data. This is a map-data-quality problem sitting upstream of the algorithm entirely: a contraction hierarchy or A* search is only as trustworthy as the graph it's built on, and production routing engines invest heavily in map data validation and driver-reported corrections precisely because the search algorithm cannot detect that an edge in its own graph shouldn't exist.

No specific Uber incident of this kind is public, so this is presented as a realistic, industry-standard failure pattern rather than a documented event. A major road — a bridge, a highway segment — closes for emergency repair. Until the routing engine's underlying graph is updated and its contraction hierarchy rebuilt (not instantaneous at continent scale, per §6), queries continue returning routes through the closed segment, because the precomputed shortcuts still assume it's passable. Drivers following those routes hit the closure and have to detour manually, and ETAs for anyone routed through that shortcut become wrong until the hierarchy catches up. The standard mitigation is exactly what §6 named: keeping topology changes (road closures, new roads) on a much faster update cycle than full hierarchy rebuilds, often via smaller incremental patches or penalty overlays applied on top of the precomputed structure rather than waiting for a full recompute.

As with dispatch, there is no public production routing-engine source to walk through cold here. What follows is illustrative reference pseudocode, representative of how a real-time, precomputed-hierarchy routing service is actually built in industry — including in real, publicly readable open-source projects like OSRM — not a reproduction of any single company's undisclosed internals.

Restricting each direction's search to edges going up in contraction rank means the search space from any node shrinks fast — a low-importance residential street node has almost no upward edges, so the search rockets toward the handful of high-importance highway-like nodes almost immediately, rather than fanning out across every nearby side street the way plain Dijkstra would. Meeting in the middle from both directions means neither search has to reach all the way to the other endpoint — it only has to reach a shared high-rank node somewhere between them, which is precisely why query cost stays close to independent of total graph size, as §10's chart shows.
Six questions, then a sequencing challenge. Wrong answers explain why they're wrong — read them, they encode the chapter.

Generate a random road-like graph, then watch Dijkstra's search frontier expand node by node from origin to destination, and compare its real visited-node count against a precomputed contraction-hierarchy-style query on the identical graph. Both numbers come from actually running each search, not a scripted animation.

1. Generate a new graph, step Dijkstra fully, note how much of the grid it touches before reaching the destination. 2. Run the shortcut-style query on the identical graph and compare touched-node counts directly — both paths should have the same or very close total cost, since both are finding a true shortest path, just at very different search cost. 3. Increase grid size and watch Dijkstra's visited-node count grow much faster than the shortcut query's — this is §10's "query cost near-independent of graph size" claim, demonstrated rather than merely asserted.

You can now explain precisely why straight-line distance and raw GPS points are the wrong inputs for ETA, why plain Dijkstra doesn't scale to real dispatch query volume, and what a contraction hierarchy actually precomputes to make queries fast — and you've watched both searches run for real on the same graph. Everything in chapters 4 and 5 assumed a fixed marketplace: a knowable number of riders and drivers, matched at a knowable price. Chapter 6 breaks that assumption on purpose — what happens to matching when demand spikes faster than supply can respond, and price becomes the mechanism doing the work.
